question.problem: By the multiplicative property of congruences, ${4}^{8}≡$
question.worked_solution:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{4}^{8}={4}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}\cdot {4}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2} & ≡16\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\cdot 7+2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\cdot 0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\ {4}^{3} & ≡4\cdot {4}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\cdot 7+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{8} & ≡{4}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\cdot 1\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{4}^{8}≡2\,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$
